candidates.title: The Lateralization and Distalization Shoulder Angles in Reverse Total Shoulder Arthroplasty Are Highly Sensitive to Both Arm Position and Viewing Angle: Analyzed Using the Enovis Altivate and Surgicase.
candidates.authors_short: Kane LT, Namdari S, Amini M
candidates.journal: Journal of shoulder and elbow surgery
candidates.abstract: BACKGROUND: In reverse total shoulder arthroplasty (rTSA), the lateralization shoulder angle (LSA) and distalization shoulder angle (DSA) are very prevalent in clinical research and clinical practice to measure the geometry of the implant construct. The purpose of this study was to determine whether LSA and DSA are impacted by changes in 1) resting arm angle (RAA) and 2) radiographic viewing angle. Secondarily, the study evaluated if linear measures of lateralization and distalization are less sensitive to these changes than LSA and DSA. METHODS: This was a computer modeling study using commercially available preoperative planning three-dimensional software (Materialise Surgicase). Ten patients without glenoid bone loss undergoing rTSA were included. Four distinct implant constructs (Enovis Altivate Reverse®) were placed in each patient, resulting in 40 total plans. For each plan, thirteen unique viewing profiles were generated to establish variability in the following measurements: LSA, DSA, humeral distalization (acromiohumeral interval (AHI)), and humeral lateralization (distance from glenosphere center of rotation to greater tuberosity (GT-COR)). For each measurement, a one-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) and Pearson's r evaluated its variability by change in viewing profile. Additionally, the humeral position and viewing angle that provided the largest discrepancy in LSA and DSA values were combined and measured to evaluate maximum variability. RESULTS: LSA measurements were significantly impacted by changes in RAA (r=0.383; p<0.001) and increases in viewing angle: medial tilt (r=0.284; p=0.006), lateral tilt (r=-0.400; p<0.001), and superior tilt (r=0.509; p<0.001). Similarly, DSA measurements were significantly altered by changes in RAA (r=-0.454; p<0.001) and viewing angle: medial tilt (r=-0.282; p=0.005), lateral tilt (r=0.419; p<0.001), and superior tilt (r=-0.328; p=0.001). Neither LSA nor DSA measurements were affected by changes in humeral rotation or inferior tilt. The difference between the smallest and largest measurements was on average 35.8° (R: 28.3°-48°) for LSA and 34.6° (R: 20.9°-52.8°) for DSA. Changes in AHI were found to be correlated with changes in RAA (r=-0.588; p<0.001) and increases in superior tilt only (r=-0.259; p=0.017). GT-COR measurements were not impacted by RAA, humeral rotation, or viewing angle. CONCLUSION: The commonly utilized parameters LSA and DSA show significant variability with and sensitivity to both arm position and viewing angle. Linear measurements of lateralization and distalization are less sensitive to these changes. LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Basic Science Study, Validation of Computer Modeling Software.
candidates.score_reasoning: International Consensus Meeting proceedings from 2025 on periprosthetic shoulder infection management, published in JSES, providing directly actionable consensus recommendations from global experts with supermajority agreement across 29 clinical questions.
bullets: LSA and DSA measurements varied by an average of 35 to 36 degrees depending on how the arm was positioned and how the X-ray was angled.
In patients undergoing reverse total shoulder arthroplasty, these angular implant measurements are unreliable unless arm position and X-ray beam direction are strictly standardized.

Linear measurements such as acromiohumeral interval and glenosphere center of rotation to greater tuberosity distance are more stable across viewing conditions and may be preferable for comparing implant geometry.

candidates.title: The Incidence of Late Periprosthetic Femoral Fractures by Implant Type-A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
candidates.authors_short: Brkljac M, Lovie J, et al.
candidates.journal: The Journal of the American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons
candidates.abstract: AIMS: Periprosthetic femoral fractures (PFF) are the leading cause of revision surgery after total hip arthroplasty when revision and fixation are combined, with morbidity and mortality akin to hip fractures. Polished taper slip (PTS) stems are increasingly seen as high risk; fracture risk of other cementation philosophies, or with noncemented stems excluding intraoperative or early postoperative fractures, remains uncertain. We compared the incidence of late PFFs (>3 months postoperatively) across different stem designs. METHODS: A systematic review of English-language studies published since 2000 was conducted. The Newcastle-Ottawa scale was used to assess study quality, with overall good ratings. A total of 28,854 hips from 27 studies were included (19,552 cemented, 9,302 noncemented). Stems were classified into subtypes to compare similar designs. Studies were excluded if early fractures (<3 months) could not be separated. RESULTS: No notable difference in late PFF risk was found between cemented and noncemented stems (incidence rate ratios: 1.00, 95% confidence interval 0.74 to 1.35). Among cemented stems, PTS designs had the highest fracture rate (0.15 per 100 person-years), markedly higher than French paradox (0.04), and composite beam stems (0.01) (P = 0.0158). Within PTS stems, CPT (0.53) and C stems (0.29) had the highest rates, whereas CPCS had the lowest (0.09). Within noncemented designs, type A stems did not show an advantage over type B (0.07 vs 0.12; P = 0.29). No difference in fracture rates between collared and noncollared noncemented implants was seen (P = 0.58 confidence interval 95% 0.53 to 1.42). CONCLUSION: Noncemented stems do not pose a higher late PFF risk than cemented stems. PTS stems show particularly high late fracture rates, with substantial variation between individual designs. By contrast, French paradox and composite beam stems appear protective and may offer a safer cemented option. No notable differences were observed among noncemented designs. Future studies should incorporate standardized methods for analyzing the relationship between the stem and femoral morphology.
candidates.score_reasoning: High-impact systematic review and meta-analysis in JAAOS clarifying late periprosthetic femoral fracture risk by implant type across 28,854 hips, with directly actionable findings distinguishing polished taper slip from other cemented stem designs.
bullets: Polished taper slip cemented stems carry the highest late periprosthetic femoral fracture rate among all implant types, more than three times higher than French paradox stems and fifteen times higher than composite beam stems.
Cemented and uncemented stems carry equivalent late fracture risk overall, so implant fixation method alone should not drive decision-making for fracture prevention in total hip arthroplasty.

For surgeons using cemented fixation, French paradox and composite beam stems appear to be safer choices than polished taper slip designs when minimizing late periprosthetic femoral fracture risk is a priority.

candidates.title: Intra-Articular Injection Into a Nonoperative Joint Within 90 Days Before Total Knee Arthroplasty is Associated With Increased Revision.
candidates.authors_short: Liao GY, Chansky H, et al.
candidates.abstract: BACKGROUND: Intra-articular injections are commonly used to manage symptomatic osteoarthritis prior to total knee arthroplasty (TKA). While injections into the operative knee have been associated with increased postoperative infection risk when performed within three months of surgery, the effect of injections into nonoperative joints remains unclear. METHODS: We conducted a retrospective cohort study using a national all-payer administrative database of patients undergoing isolated primary TKA. The primary exposure was an intra-articular injection into a nonoperative joint within 90 days before surgery. Patients who had ipsilateral knee injections were excluded from the main analysis. The final cohort comprised 1,074,331 patients, of whom 5,419 (0.5%) received a nonoperative joint injection within 90 days before TKA. The primary outcome was all-cause revision at 90 days, six months, and one year. The secondary outcomes included etiology-specific revision. Multivariable Cox proportional hazards models were used to evaluate associations. RESULTS: Injection was associated with higher unadjusted revision rates at one year (1.25 versus 0.80%) and remained associated with increased revision hazard after adjustment at one year (hazard ratio [HR], 1.43) and six months (HR, 1.52), but not at 90 days. Etiology-specific analyses demonstrated that this association was primarily driven by periprosthetic joint infection (PJI), with increased hazard at one year (HR, 1.40). There were no consistent associations observed for mechanical loosening, instability, or periprosthetic fracture after adjustment. CONCLUSIONS: Intra-articular injection into a nonoperative, non-knee joint within 90 days before TKA was associated with an increased risk of revision, driven primarily by revision for PJI. These findings suggest that recent injection into a nonoperative, non-knee joint may be relevant to perioperative risk assessment, although the underlying mechanism remains uncertain.
candidates.score_reasoning: Large-scale retrospective cohort study in Journal of Arthroplasty examining Xa inhibitor versus aspirin VTE prophylaxis and manipulation under anesthesia risk in 435,789 TKA patients, with highly actionable findings for perioperative anticoagulation decision-making.
bullets: Patients who received an injection into a non-operative joint within 90 days before total knee arthroplasty had a 43% higher revision rate at one year compared to those who did not.
The increased revision risk was driven almost entirely by periprosthetic joint infection, not mechanical failure, instability, or fracture.
Surgeons should factor in recent injections to any joint, not just the operative knee, when counseling patients and assessing perioperative infection risk before TKA.

candidates.title: Stratified Diagnostic Thresholds by Infection Chronicity Resolve the Controversy in Unicompartmental Knee Arthroplasty Periprosthetic Joint Infection: A Prospective Study.
candidates.authors_short: Zhang Z, Huang Q, et al.
candidates.abstract: BACKGROUND: Diagnosing periprosthetic joint infection (PJI) in unicompartmental knee arthroplasty (UKA) is complicated by the "hybrid joint" environment and contradictory literature thresholds that overlook infection chronicity. We aimed to define chronicity-stratified thresholds for standard markers and evaluate the diagnostic utility of synovial neutrophil gelatinase-associated lipocalin (NGAL) in this specific context. METHODS: There were 77 revision UKA patients (20 acute PJI, 19 chronic, and 38 aseptic) prospectively enrolled. A PJI was defined by Musculoskeletal Infection Society (MSIS)/International Consensus Meeting (ICM) criteria and stratified by Tsukayama classification (less than four weeks: acute; greater than four weeks: chronic). Synovial fluid white blood cell (SF-WBC), polymorphonuclear neutrophil (%PMN), and NGAL were analyzed via receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curves to determine optimal cutoffs. RESULTS: Acute PJI exhibited high inflammatory baselines (SF-WBC greater than 10,020/μL, area under the curve [AUC] 0.976; PMN% greater than 81.0%), whereas chronic PJI required significantly lower cutoffs (SF-WBC less than 2,770/μL, AUC 0.958; PMN% greater than 62.0%). Synovial NGAL demonstrated robust stability (Acute: greater than 274 ng/mL, AUC 0.995; Chronic: greater than 174 ng/mL, AUC 0.992), notably achieving 100% sensitivity in chronic cases. High-virulence organisms predominated in acute cases (35.0% Staphylococcus aureus [S. aureus]), contrasting with low-virulence organisms in chronic infections (42.1% Coagulase-negative staphylococci [CoNS]). CONCLUSIONS: In this preliminary single-center cohort, ROC-derived synovial fluid cutoff estimates differed between acute and chronic UKA-PJI. These findings suggest that infection chronicity may be relevant when interpreting synovial biomarkers in failed UKA. Synovial NGAL showed promising diagnostic performance in both subgroups; however, its optimal cutoff estimates also differed by chronicity. Larger multicenter studies with independent external validation are required before these exploratory thresholds can be recommended for routine clinical use.
candidates.score_reasoning: Prospective study in Journal of Arthroplasty establishing chronicity-stratified diagnostic thresholds for UKA PJI with novel synovial NGAL biomarker achieving near-perfect AUC, directly addressing a controversial diagnostic gap for a growing surgical population.
bullets: In revision UKA, infection timing matters: acute PJI requires a synovial WBC above 10,020 per microliter for diagnosis, while chronic PJI is flagged at a much lower threshold below 2,770 per microliter.
Synovial NGAL outperformed standard markers in this cohort, reaching 100% sensitivity for chronic UKA infection at a cutoff above 174 ng/mL.
Surgeons evaluating a failed UKA should not apply standard TKA PJI thresholds directly, as chronicity significantly shifts the diagnostic cutoffs for all synovial biomarkers tested.

candidates.title: Operative Strategies for Treating Tibial Plateau Fractures in Patients Aged 55 Years and Older: A Five-Year Comparison of Acute Total Knee Arthroplasty with Open Reduction and Internal Fixation, Conversion Total Knee Arthroplasty, and Total Knee Arthroplasty for Osteoarthritis.
candidates.authors_short: Wahid M, Bellamy J, et al.
candidates.abstract: OBJECTIVES: To compare outcomes of acute total knee arthroplasty (TKA) for tibial plateau fracture in patients aged 55 years and older with matched patients undergoing open reduction and internal fixation (ORIF), conversion TKA after failed ORIF, and primary TKA for osteoarthritis. METHODS: Design: Retrospective cohort study with propensity score matching. SETTING: Federated multi-institutional electronic health records database (TriNetX United States Collaborative Network). PATIENT SELECTION CRITERIA: Patients aged ≥55 years with tibial plateau fracture treated with acute TKA, ORIF, or conversion TKA after failed ORIF were identified. A separate cohort undergoing primary TKA for osteoarthritis without fracture history was identified as a non-traumatic comparator. The study period was restricted to January 1, 2005 through December 31, 2020 to ensure a minimum of five years of potential follow-up for all included patients. OUTCOME MEASURES AND COMPARISONS: The primary outcome was revision surgery at 5 years, defined as conversion to TKA after ORIF and as revision TKA after arthroplasty. Secondary outcomes were a composite "return to the operating room (OR)" outcome (selected major reoperations), periprosthetic joint infection (PJI), surgical site infection (SSI), aseptic loosening, manipulation under anesthesia (MUA), and periprosthetic fracture. Three 1:1 propensity score-matched comparisons were performed (acute TKA versus ORIF; acute versus conversion TKA; acute TKA versus primary TKA for osteoarthritis), with risk ratios (RR) and 95% confidence intervals (CI) calculated. Subgroup analyses were stratified by age (55-70 years; ≥70 years). RESULTS: After matching, 1,321 patients per cohort were compared in the primary acute TKA versus ORIF analysis. Mean age was 66.1 years in the acute TKA cohort and 66.6 years in the ORIF cohort (range, 55 to 90 in both), and 65.3% and 66.7%, respectively, were female. Acute TKA had higher 5-year revision rates than ORIF (7.0% versus 0.8%; RR 8.36, 95% CI 4.50-15.56; P < 0.001) and elevated PJI rates (6.2% versus 1.3%; RR 4.82, 95% CI 2.88-8.09; P < 0.001). Return to OR rates did not differ significantly between acute TKA and ORIF (25.6% versus 23.5%; RR 1.09, 95% CI 0.95-1.25; P = 0.21). Revision did not differ between acute and conversion TKA (9.0% versus 10.0%; RR 0.89, 95% CI 0.58-1.35; P = 0.589) but was higher after acute TKA than after primary TKA for osteoarthritis (7.4% versus 3.5%; RR 2.12, 95% CI 1.48-3.00; P < 0.001). Revision was higher after acute TKA than ORIF in patients aged 55-70 years (9.3% versus 1.7%; RR 5.41, 95% CI 2.80-10.48; P < 0.001) and was not reportable in those aged ≥70 years owing to small cell counts. CONCLUSIONS: In patients aged 55 years and older, acute TKA for tibial plateau fracture was associated with higher risks of revision and complications compared with ORIF. Revision and complication rates after acute TKA were comparable with those after conversion TKA following failed ORIF but higher than those after primary TKA for osteoarthritis. Acute TKA should be reserved for patients at highest risk of ORIF failure requiring subsequent conversion to TKA. LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level III, therapeutic study.
candidates.score_reasoning: Journal of Orthopaedic Trauma retrospective cohort comparing acute TKA, ORIF, conversion TKA, and primary TKA for tibial plateau fractures in patients ≥55 years using propensity-matched TriNetX data, addressing a high-stakes operative decision with multi-arm comparisons.
bullets: In patients aged 55 and older with tibial plateau fractures, acute TKA carried a much higher 5-year revision rate than ORIF (7.0% vs 0.8%) and nearly five times the rate of periprosthetic joint infection.
Revision rates after acute TKA were similar to those after conversion TKA for failed ORIF, meaning upfront arthroplasty does not reliably spare patients from reoperation risk.

ORIF should remain the default fixation strategy for tibial plateau fractures in older patients, with acute TKA reserved for those where ORIF failure and subsequent conversion are considered near certain.

candidates.title: Nonoperative Management Deserves Consideration for Select Patients with Valgus-Impacted Femoral Neck Fractures.
candidates.journal: The Journal of bone and joint surgery. American volume
candidates.abstract: The valgus-impacted femoral neck fracture is unique among hip fractures. Patients are often relatively comfortable, and the fracture pattern is inherently more stable than other femoral neck fracture types. In situ fixation remains the default treatment for most surgeons, and this remains a reasonable approach, particularly for patients unable to reliably protect their weight-bearing. However, multiple randomized controlled trials and meta-analyses have revealed that, when surgery is chosen, arthroplasty carries a lower risk of reoperation and implant-related complications than fixation, with no difference in mortality. Additionally, nonoperative management has achieved rates of uneventful healing comparable with those of fixation in appropriately selected patients who were able to protect their weight-bearing, and delayed arthroplasty after failed nonoperative treatment has not been associated with excess morbidity compared with acute arthroplasty across measured outcomes. Given that fixation in situ may not have dramatically better efficacy than nonoperative care and that failed nonoperative management can be salvaged with delayed arthroplasty without excess morbidity, we propose that nonoperative management is a reasonable initial treatment for select patients. The best candidates are patients who are cognitively intact, living independently, and medically stable and who are reasonably comfortable and capable of mobilizing while protecting their weight-bearing. Close clinical and radiographic follow-up is required, with a low threshold for conversion to arthroplasty in the setting of uncontrolled pain, poor mobilization, or radiographic evidence of loss of reduction. Dementia, high comorbidity burden, and assisted living status are associated with failure of nonoperative management. In all circumstances, both fixation and acute arthroplasty remain valid alternative strategies. We advocate a shared decision-making approach that accounts for the risks and benefits of all treatment strategies as well as patient factors.
candidates.score_reasoning: JBJS review challenging the default of in-situ fixation for valgus-impacted femoral neck fractures by synthesizing RCT and meta-analysis evidence supporting nonoperative management as a viable option, with significant practice-changing implications.
bullets: In cognitively intact, independently living patients with valgus-impacted femoral neck fractures, nonoperative management achieves healing rates comparable to in situ fixation when weight-bearing precautions can be reliably followed.
If nonoperative management fails, delayed arthroplasty carries no additional morbidity compared to acute arthroplasty, making it a viable salvage option.
Dementia, high comorbidity burden, and assisted living status predict nonoperative failure, and these patients should be steered toward surgical treatment from the outset.

candidates.title: Clinical and Radiographic Outcomes of Suture Anchor Repair versus Transarticular Kirschner Wire Fixation of the Acromioclavicular Joint in Acute High-grade Dislocation: A Randomized Clinical Trial.
candidates.authors_short: Hirunthanawiwat T, Benjawongsathien K, et al.
candidates.journal: Journal of shoulder and elbow surgery
candidates.abstract: BACKGROUND: For high-grade acromioclavicular (AC) joint injury, repairing the AC ligament complex in addition to coracoclavicular (CC) stabilization provides superior biomechanical and functional outcomes. Rigid AC fixation, such as transarticular wires or hook plates, yields reliable outcomes but may be offset by complications. Therefore, this study compared the clinical and radiographic outcomes of an alternative AC stabilization with Suture anchor repair versus K-wire fixation. METHODS: A prospective randomized trial was conducted in 32 patients with acute AC dislocation. Patients were randomized (16 per group) to Suture anchor repair or transarticular K-wire fixation, both with the same nonbiologic CC suspensory technique. In the Suture anchor group, a single 2.8-mm anchor was inserted into the distal clavicle to repair the superior AC capsuloligamentous complex. The primary outcome was the Constant-Murley Score (CMS); secondary outcomes were the American Shoulder and Elbow Surgeons (ASES) and University of California, Los Angeles (UCLA) shoulder scores, percentage coracoclavicular distance (%CCD) change, and complications, assessed at 4, 8, 16, 24, and 52 weeks. Repeated measurements were analyzed using multilevel Gaussian regression with Bonferroni adjustment, and differences were interpreted against published minimal clinically important difference thresholds. RESULTS: All 32 patients completed 52-week follow-up. The Suture anchor group included 3 Rockwood type IIIB and 13 type V, while the K-wire group included 8 type IIIB and 8 type V. The Suture anchor group had higher CMS at 4 weeks (mean difference, 12.7 points; 95% CI, 8.7-16.6), 8 weeks (7.9; 95% CI, 4.0-11.9), and 16 weeks (5.3; 95% CI, 1.4-9.3) (all P ≤ .003), with no difference at 24 or 52 weeks. ASES and UCLA scores were higher in the Suture anchor group at 4 and 8 weeks only (all P < .001). The K-wire group, after wire removal at 4 weeks, showed a smaller %CCD change at every interval, with a mean loss of 4.6% versus 14.5% at 52 weeks (mean difference, 9.9%; 95% CI, 3.4-16.4; P < .001). Complications occurred in 4 K-wire patients (25.0%; 4 pin migrations, 1 with superficial pin-tract infection) and in no Suture anchor patients (P = .101). CONCLUSION: While AC stabilization with suture anchor repair provided faster early functional recovery and K-wire fixation better maintained radiographic reduction, both techniques yielded comparable functional outcomes from 24 weeks and onward. Additionally, these findings should be limited to AC joint dislocation with primarily vertical instability, and the choice between techniques should be individualized. LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level I, Randomized Controlled Trial, Treatment Study.
candidates.score_reasoning: Prospective RCT in JSES comparing suture anchor repair versus K-wire fixation for high-grade AC joint dislocation with 32 patients and 52-week follow-up, providing direct comparative data for a commonly debated surgical technique choice.
bullets: In adults with acute high-grade AC joint dislocation, suture anchor repair gave faster shoulder function recovery in the first 16 weeks, but both techniques reached the same functional scores by 24 weeks.
K-wire fixation maintained better radiographic reduction at one year, but carried a 25% complication rate from pin migration and infection, while suture anchor repair had none.
Either technique is reasonable for AC dislocations with primarily vertical instability, and the choice should be based on patient factors and surgeon preference given equivalent one-year outcomes.

candidates.title: What Are the Long-term Outcomes of Periacetabular Osteotomy in a United States Cohort?
candidates.authors_short: Maroyan A, Mendola LC, et al.
candidates.abstract: BACKGROUND: Periacetabular osteotomy (PAO) is an effective and common hip-preserving procedure used to treat symptomatic acetabular dysplasia of the hip. Evidence regarding long-term outcomes after PAO remains limited. Information regarding long-term outcomes may be important in developing reasonable expectations for both patients and surgeons to facilitate effective therapeutic decision-making. QUESTIONS/PURPOSES: (1) What is the likelihood of long-term hip preservation and the level of pain at a minimum of 25 years of follow-up after PAO? (2) What clinical and radiographic factors were associated with patients having a poor result, which we defined either as having THA or a WOMAC score of ≥ 10 points at the most recent survey? (3) What were the outcome scores of patients who underwent THA after PAO, and how did these scores compare to the scores of the preserved hips and to the scores of age-related norms? METHODS: We retrospectively evaluated the cohort of the first 142 patients (171 hips) who underwent PAO performed by one surgeon to treat symptomatic dysplasia between 1991 and 1998. Twenty-three percent (33 of 142) of patients (37 hips) were lost to follow-up. This included six patients (6 hips) who had died, 23 patients (26 hips) who could not be located, and four patients (5 hips) who did not complete questionnaires. Seventy-seven percent (109 of 142) of eligible patients (134 hips) returned complete questionnaires at a median (range) of 27 years (25 to 33) after PAO. Our analyzed group included 87% female patients (95 patients, 117 hips) and 13% male patients (14 patients, 17 hips). The median (range) age at surgery was 25 years (9 to 45). The median (range) time of review after PAO was 27 years (25 to 33). The 53 hips that had undergone THA were reviewed at a median (range) of 11 years (1 to 28) after the THA. Kaplan-Meier analysis was used to assess survivorship free from conversion to THA. Hips were postoperatively evaluated using the pain subscale of the WOMAC index. We characterized a poor clinical outcome as either having a preserved hip with a WOMAC pain score of ≥ 10 or undergoing THA. All patients who were analyzed returned questionnaires; some were seen in person with images. Factors associated with a patient having a high (poor) WOMAC score for pain or undergoing THA were evaluated using a multinomial logistic regression model using generalized estimating equations. RESULTS: Of patients analyzed, 60% (81 of 134) of hips remained preserved. Forty percent (53 of 134) of hips had undergone THA at a median of 22 years after PAO. The survivorship free from conversion to THA at 25 years after PAO was 70% (95% confidence interval [CI] 62% to 78%), and the median (range) level of pain was 1 (0 to 20) of 20 points. After controlling for potentially confounding variables including sex, preoperative lateral center-edge angle and anterior center-edge angle, and postoperative lateral center-edge angle, we found that the following factors were associated with increased odds of having either a poor (≥ 10 points) WOMAC pain score or conversion to THA: preoperative joint space width ≤ 2 mm (HR 7.3 [95% CI 2.8 to 19.2]), labral tear noted intraoperatively (HR 2.8 [95% CI 1.3 to 5.8]), age at surgery > 21 years and < 35 years (HR 2.6 [95% CI 1.1 to 5.9]), and age at surgery ≥ 35 years (HR 3.4 [95% CI 1.1 to 11.0]). In patients who underwent THA, the median (range) WOMAC score was 1 (0 to 20) (lower scores represent less pain and better function), the median (range) modified Harris hip score was 85 (7 to 91) points (higher scores represent less pain and better function), and the median (range) HOOS pain score was 95 (0 to 100). The mean University of California, Los Angeles (UCLA) activity level score for the THA group was 6. In general, these scores did not differ by clinically important margins when compared with the hips that had not undergone THA or compared with age-related score norms. CONCLUSION: While a majority of hips can be preserved with good function at a mean of 27 years after PAO, our findings suggest that surgery should be considered as soon as the diagnosis of symptomatic dysplasia is made, given that older age at the time of surgery was independently associated with later THA or a WOMAC pain score of ≥ 10. If a patient develops painful arthrosis after a PAO, THA should be offered and expected to provide function comparable to age-related norms. Prospective registry-based multicenter studies of patients treated for symptomatic hip dysplasia are indicated to improve outcomes. LEVEL OF EVIDENCE LEVEL: III, therapeutic study.
candidates.score_reasoning: Journal of Arthroplasty retrospective cohort on PAO outcomes at minimum 25-year follow-up in 109 patients, providing rare long-term data on hip preservation surgery outcomes that inform patient counseling and surgical decision-making for dysplasia.
bullets: At 27-year follow-up, 70% of hips treated with periacetabular osteotomy for dysplasia were preserved without conversion to total hip arthroplasty, and preserved hips had low pain scores.
Narrowed preoperative joint space (2 mm or less), intraoperative labral tear, and age over 21 at surgery were each independently associated with worse outcomes or eventual hip replacement.

Patients who did eventually need total hip arthroplasty after periacetabular osteotomy achieved pain and function scores comparable to age-matched population norms, so conversion should not be delayed when arthrosis becomes symptomatic.

candidates.title: CORR Insights®: What Do National Joint Replacement Registries Fail to Collect? The Critical Value of Recording Preoperative Alignment for Prediction of Revision After TKA: A Nested-model Analysis of Registry-only versus Seldom- and Never-recorded Variables.
candidates.score_reasoning: Journal of Arthroplasty large database study of over 1 million TKA patients demonstrating that nonoperative joint injections within 90 days before TKA increase PJI-driven revision risk, with novel and clinically actionable perioperative management implications.
bullets: Preoperative knee alignment is not routinely captured in national joint registries, leaving a key predictor of TKA revision risk unrecorded.
Adding preoperative alignment data to registry models improves prediction of which TKA patients will go on to need revision surgery.
Orthopaedic registries should collect preoperative alignment to better identify high-risk patients and guide implant and technique decisions.

candidates.title: Antibiotic Nails Outperform Implant Retention in Preventing Recurrent Infections After Intramedullary Nail Fixation of Tibial Shaft Fractures Complicated by Infection.
candidates.authors_short: Wilhelm ZC, Kommu K, et al.
candidates.abstract: OBJECTIVES: To compare infection recurrence rates between patients treated with antibiotic nail versus implant retention for open tibial shaft fractures initially treated with an intramedullary (IM) nail complicated by infection. METHODS: Design: Retrospective cohort study. SETTING: Level I trauma center. PATIENT SELECTION CRITERIA: Adults with tibial shaft fractures (OTA/AO 42A-C) treated with an IM nail between 2007 and 2023 who developed deep surgical site infections after index fixation were included. OUTCOME MEASURES AND COMPARISONS: The primary outcome was infection recurrence within 2 years requiring reoperation and antibiotics. Secondary outcomes included amputation rate, all-cause mortality rate, days in hospital within 1 year of index infection surgery, time to recurrence, and number of surgeries needed after recurrence. The association between treatment and the study outcomes was estimated using Cox proportional hazards models, controlling for potential confounders. RESULTS: A total of 96 patients were included, 75 (78%) [62 males; median age 47 years (interquartile range (IQR), 31 to 53)] were treated with conversion to antibiotic nail and 21 (22%) [18 males; median age 36 years (IQR, 27 to 48)] with implant retention. The antibiotic nail group was more likely to have chronic infections, requiring surgery 6 or more weeks after index IM nail fixation (65% vs. 38%, P = 0.03). The 2-year infection recurrence rate was significantly lower with implant removal and antibiotic nail (33%) than with implant retention (54%) (HR, 0.43; 95% CI, 0.20 to 0.92; P = 0.03). For the secondary outcomes collected, only the average number of surgeries required after recurrence differed significantly between the two groups, with 3.9 for antibiotic nail and 3.0 for implant retention (IRR, 1.39; 95% CI, 1.01 to 1.91; P = 0.04). CONCLUSIONS: Conversion to an antibiotic nail was associated with lower rates of infection recurrence compared with implant retention. The overall infection recurrence rates of 33% in the antibiotic nail cohort and 54% in the implant retention cohort highlight the challenges associated with treating infection after IM nail fixation of tibial shaft fractures, regardless of treatment strategy. LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Therapeutic, Level III.
candidates.score_reasoning: Journal of Orthopaedic Trauma secondary analysis of two prospective RCTs at 25 institutions evaluating timing of flap coverage and infection risk in open fractures, providing high-quality evidence on a critical intraoperative decision with infection prevention implications.
bullets: In infected tibial IM nails, converting to an antibiotic nail cut 2-year infection recurrence from 54% to 33% compared with keeping the original implant.
This applies to adult patients who develop deep infection after tibial shaft fracture fixation, including those with chronic infections presenting more than 6 weeks out.
Antibiotic nail conversion is the preferred treatment strategy for infected tibial IM nails, though one in three patients will still have recurrent infection requiring reoperation.
